documents: Nasim S, Oussalah M, Klöve B, Haghighi AT (2022) Machine learning model for snow depth estimation using a multisensory ubiquitous platform. J. Mt. Sci. 19(9): 2506-2527 (published PDF)

entry.evidence: The advances in ubiquitous and wearable technology promote new prospects in tackling this challenge.

sequences.source_document: Nasim et al. 2022, J. Mt. Sci. 19(9): 2506-2527 (published PDF)

steps.action: Pose the problem that local-scale snow depth estimation lacks accuracy and flexibility despite remote sensing advances.
steps.quote: the estimation of snow depth at local scale still requires improved [...]

steps.action: Review existing snow depth technologies (manual, ultrasonic, satellite, SAR, LiDAR, UAV, WSN) and cite Dozier et al. on the unsolved status of spatial SWE estimation.
steps.quote: spatial snow water equivalent estimation as currently the most important unsolved problem in snow hydrology

steps.action: Build on the authors' earlier foot-based wearable platform used for vegetation height estimation.
steps.quote: building on our previous work (Nasim et al. 2020)

steps.action: Hypothesize, by analogy with touch sensing, that foot-borne pressure, acoustic and temperature sensing carry information on snow depth.
steps.quote: we hypothesize that snow properties, including snow depth, can be approached by exploring the foot sensing modalities

steps.action: Select a study region near Oulu with varied snow depth, four sub-regions and 90 sites, and run experiments in March under fresh snowfall.
steps.quote: we carried out our experiments during March period

steps.action: Assemble the wearable platform: Arduino Uno, DHT22 temperature/humidity sensor, MAX9814 microphone, Tekscan FlexiForce A201 force sensor and HC-05 Bluetooth link to an Android app.
steps.quote: The designed wearable platform consists of three sensors and a microcontroller

steps.action: Calibrate the force sensor by fitting a linear voltage-force relation to input-output measurements (Vo = 0.0278 pressure + 0.75).
steps.quote: a voltage- force graph is plotted where the best linear fit is identified

steps.action: Design the protocol: a 10 m random walk of about 30 s and 34 footsteps per site, with yardstick depth at four points 2.5 m apart and a snow sample for density, repeated at 90 sites.
steps.quote: in total 90 similar experiments were run at different paths to generate 90 samples for dataset preparation

steps.action: Record footstep pressure, sound, temperature and humidity with the platform, extract max/min/mean features after min-max normalisation, and measure averaged ground-truth snow depth (13-40 cm) and density.
steps.quote: The user, equipped with the wearable footwear, performs a random walk for around 30 seconds on average.

steps.action: Drop temperature and humidity as discriminating variables because they stayed constant across sites during the short campaign.
steps.quote: both of them cannot be contribute to distinguish among snow depth measurements

steps.action: Compute Pearson correlations between sensor features and snow depth; max pressure correlates strongly and negatively (r = -0.84), min pressure partly, the others weakly or not at all.
steps.quote: the max pressure indicates a strong statistically negative correlation with snow depth r (90) = -0.84, n = 90

steps.action: Explain the negative pressure-depth relation as deeper snow making walking harder and lowering the recorded pressure.
steps.quote: high snow level above the surface creates difficult walking conditions for the user, which result in a lower recording of pressure values

steps.action: Check the correlations with single-variable linear regressions (max pressure R2 = 0.83) and a two-variable OLS (R2 = 0.744), which does not outperform the single variable.
steps.quote: To validate and verify the results and test the variables relevance, we also applied a regression model

steps.action: Recast estimation as classification into six 5 cm snow-depth classes (14-16 samples each), citing difficulty of fine-grained continuous estimation.
steps.quote: a subdivision on the snow depth measurements is created and tested

steps.action: Screen a bench of scikit-learn classifiers at default settings on all features; Random Forest, SVM and k-NN emerge as top performers.
steps.quote: we initially run a bench of machine learning classification algorithms available from a typical machine learning library such as scikit

steps.action: Train Random Forest on 72 samples, test on 18 (accuracy 0.89), and rank feature importance; pressure features are most relevant and acoustic features unreliable.
steps.quote: The classifier was trained on the 72 samples and tested on 18 samples.

steps.action: Grid-search n_estimators and max_depth with validation curves; tuning changes accuracy only marginally and reveals overfitting.
steps.quote: the validation curve revealed overfitting of our model

steps.action: After the overfitting, switch to K-fold cross-validation with tuning of n_estimators, max_depth and min_samples_leaf on a reduced two-feature matrix.
steps.quote: to overcome this issue we employed another strategy known as K-fold cross-validation

steps.action: Recompute cross-validated RF accuracy across top-k feature subsets; the top two features give 94%.
steps.quote: Top two subset of feature matrix achieved the highest accuracy score of 94%.

steps.action: Tune and compare SVC (linear and nonlinear kernels) and k-NN (k = 3) against RF across feature sets; RF outperforms both in all runs.
steps.quote: RF classifier has outperformed SVC and K-NN in all runs

steps.action: Compare RF trained on sub-region data alone (below 50% accuracy) with RF trained on the pooled dataset (89%).
steps.quote: training RF with overall dataset is more beneficial, yielding an overall accuracy of 89% on the four sites

steps.action: Retain the claim that the low-cost footwear platform with an RF classifier gives a relatively good snow-depth estimate, at 94% accuracy.
steps.quote: Random Forest classifier has been shown to yield state-of-the-art classification result of 94% accuracy

steps.action: Attribute the inconsistent acoustic results to the low-cost sensor and user dependence to class-difference learning, rather than revising the sensing hypothesis.
steps.quote: we believe that this limitation is mainly caused by the limited performance

Kept: platform feasible, RF 94% (CV) or 88.8% accuracy

end.claim: A foot-worn IoT platform with pressure and acoustic sensors, with a Random Forest classifier on max/min pressure features, classifies snow depth into 5 cm classes at about 94% cross-validated accuracy at the Oulu study sites.

decisive_move.sentence: Building the foot-wearable platform with a calibrated force sensor produced the max-pressure signal on which the correlation and the classifier rest.

gates.evidence: The stated hypothesis that foot sensing carries snow information (p. 2510) motivated building the platform and collecting all four sensor streams, but no discriminating acquisition was designed. The classifier faced held-out test samples and 5-fold-style cross-validation it could have failed (SVC 66%, k-NN lower, sub-region training below 50%). However, features, hyperparameters and the class scheme were chosen after seeing the data, and tuning used the same 80/20 split (p. 2521). Nothing was fixed in advance.

imports.item: Random Forest, support vector machine and k-nearest neighbour classifiers via scikit-learn, with grid search and K-fold cross-validation
Arduino Uno microcontroller, HC-05 Bluetooth, DHT22, MAX9814 microphone, Tekscan FlexiForce A201 force-sensitive resistor
Plantar force/pressure sensing, described as common in medical fields
Touch-sensing analogy: recognizing an object by touching its parts

Force /Pressure sensor, although commonly applied in other fields, e.g., medical is almost inexistent in remote environment monitoring studies

limits: The paper reports inconsistent headline numbers: 94% (abstract, p. 2522, p. 2524), 88.8% (conclusion, p. 2526) and 72.80% for RF on all features (Table 12) versus 0.89 (Table 10). The stated SVC-RF gap of 34.5% (p. 2523) does not match 66% versus 88.8%. The Discussion and Conclusion name max and mean pressure as significant, but the correlation matrix gives mean pressure r = -0.021 (Fig. 12c). The text names max and min pressure for the OLS, while Table 8 lists Maxpressure and Meanpressure. The Fig. 6 caption refers to deposition data from Cui (2007), which looks like a copy error. Inference: several runs of values in Table 4 repeat across sub-regions (e.g. sites 72-78 equal sites 14-20; sites 83-90 equal sites 52-59; sites 38-45 equal sites 2-9), which raises a question about data independence that the paper does not address. The 140 km2 area is inconsistent with coordinates spanning under 1 km. The test set has 18 samples, and hyperparameters were tuned on the same train/test split, so the accuracy may be optimistic. A single user, a single period and one location were used; the authors list portability across users, time and sites as open (p. 2524-2525). No comparison with an independent snow-depth method (LiDAR, ultrasonic) was performed, despite the framing. Sub-claim statuses: the negative max pressure to depth relation is regularity_in_range (13-40 cm, fresh snow, one user); the walking-difficulty explanation is untested (no status); the acoustic sensing hypothesis has no conclusion. No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded.

disagreements.target: LiDAR and large-scale wireless sensor networks as state-of-the-art snow depth estimation
disagreements.support: The authors argue on cost and labour grounds that their cheap platform is an alternative, but they perform no side-by-side comparison with LiDAR or WSN data.
disagreements.quote: which contrasts with popular LiDAR or expensive large scale wireless sensor network

disagreements.target: Imaging and radar-based technologies and WSN (low spatial resolution, high operational cost)
disagreements.support: The limitations of satellite and radar methods and the maintenance burden of WSN are asserted from the literature and motivate the platform; no measurement test is offered.
disagreements.quote: Our study aims to overcome the challenges of low spatial resolution of imaging and radar-based technologies and high operational cost of WSN
